sections.sourceNote: Original literary narrative written for Grade 1 Florida B.E.S.T. ELA practice.
paragraphs: Tess had to take her library book back to school. She looked on her desk, but it was not there. "Oh no!" Tess cried. She checked under her bed and in her closet. The book about tall trees was lost.

Tess felt sad and worried. Her brother Sam came into the room to help search. They peeked behind the blue chair by the window. Sam spotted a green corner in a toy bin! Tess pulled out the missing book and smiled wide.
She put the book right in her red backpack. Then Tess walked into the sunny kitchen with Sam. "We found it just in time!" she cheered. Now Tess was ready to return her book.

passages.title: Florida Manatees in Winter Springs

sections.label: Passage 1
sections.title: Warm Shelters in Cold Months
sections.sourceNote: Original Grade 3 informational text written for Florida B.E.S.T. ELA practice.
paragraphs: Every winter, hundreds of Florida manatees make a long trip. These gentle sea mammals swim away from the cool ocean water. They move into warm rivers and freshwater springs across the state. Manatees look big and round, yet they get cold fast. Unlike whales or seals, they have very little fat to keep warm. When water gets too cold, they can soon get sick. Warm water helps them stay alive in the cold months.

Florida springs give them a safe shelter in the cold months. Deep underground rocks heat the water before it bubbles up. Even on icy days, the water stays near seventy-two degrees all year. This steady warmth acts like a giant heated pool for them. Blue Spring State Park is one famous winter home for manatees. More than five hundred of them can gather in its clear, shallow water.

Inside the springs, manatees spend most of their time just resting. They float near the sandy bottom to save energy. Every few minutes, a manatee rises slowly for a breath of air. Few water plants grow in the springs, so food is scarce there. On warmer afternoons, they swim out to nearby rivers to eat. They graze on beds of green seagrass in the river water. Then they swim back before the night air cools the river.

People work hard to protect manatees in these winter habitats. At state parks, ropes block boats and swimmers from entering spring zones. Quiet zones keep the resting animals calm and safe from boat blades. Park rangers also count the manatees each morning to check on them. Researchers use tags and scars to tell each one apart. By guarding these warm springs, people help them stay safe until spring.

sections.label: Passage 1 (Primary Source)
sections.title: Excerpt from Keeper Maria Mestre de los Dolores’s Notebook, 1859
sections.authorByline: Adapted Original Historical Diary Entry (Simulated Primary Account)
sections.sourceNote: Original Fictionalized Firsthand Account · Grade 4 Paired Set
paragraphs: October 14, 1859 — Before sunset, a northeast wind began rattling the brass latches inside the St. Augustine tower. My father always said a keeper must trust her ears as much as her eyes. By dusk, salt spray tapped against the curved glass panes like impatient fingers. That sound reminded me that coastal ships depend on our steady beam.

Each evening I climb the winding iron steps with a heavy copper can of lard oil. Trimming the woven cotton wicks takes calm hands. If a wick burns unevenly, black soot clouds the precious glass prisms. Tonight the storm gusted fiercely. Still, as I lit the central lamp, amber light spilled across the dark Atlantic breakers like a golden ribbon guiding sailors safely home.

sections.label: Passage 2 (Secondary Source)
sections.title: Guarding the First Coast: The Science of Early Lighthouses
sections.sourceNote: Original Informational Article · Secondary Historical Account
paragraphs: During the nineteenth century, Florida’s Atlantic shoreline posed serious hazards for wooden ships. Shifting sandbars and shallow reefs waited just beneath the waves near St. Augustine. To warn captains away from danger, lighthouses used a remarkable optical invention called the Fresnel lens. This beehive-shaped frame of concentric glass prisms focused a single flame into a beam visible for miles.

Maintaining that beacon demanded exhausting daily labor. Keepers hauled gallons of fuel oil up narrow spiral staircases and polished hundreds of glass edges. Every few hours, they wound heavy clockwork weights so the revolving lens never stalled. Automated electric lamps replaced oil burners in the twentieth century. Still, historical records show that early keepers’ careful routines saved countless ships along Florida’s coast.

sections.title: How Sawgrass Survives in the River of Grass
sections.sourceNote: Original Informational Text · Grade 3 Science & Florida Habitats
paragraphs: South Florida holds a wide, shallow sheet of moving water called the Everglades. Visitors gaze at miles of tall, gold-green blades swaying in the warm breeze. Many assume they see ordinary marsh grass. Most of that vast sea is sawgrass. This tough, sharp-edged sedge has shaped the Everglades ecosystem for thousands of years.

Look close at the edge of one sawgrass blade. You will soon spot how the plant got its name. Tiny, sawlike teeth line both sides of each leaf. Those stiff ridges shield the plant from hungry marsh grazers. They also catch morning dew and guide rain down to the roots. Under the dark, muddy peat, thick stems store energy even when the dry season leaves the ground cracked and parched.

For years, many folks thought every marsh fire was a bad event. They feared fire ruined wild homes for good. Scientists later learned the truth. Sawgrass hides live buds safe under wet mud. Mild winter fires burn off dead thatch without hurting those roots. Soon after the smoke clears, new green shoots push up through the ash. Bright sun reaches the water again for wading birds and small fish.

Today, park rangers plan prescribed burns in cool winter months. Winds stay mild and predictable then. Crews check damp soil and weather maps before each burn. Their careful steps help sawgrass marshes stay fresh and thick. What once looked like ruin turns out to be a dependable tool for keeping Florida’s River of Grass healthy.

sections.label: Article
sections.title: Shade That Works Overtime: Why Cities Need Native Tree Canopies
sections.sourceNote: Original Informational Argument · Grade 5 Science & Civics
paragraphs: Step onto a wide asphalt lot on a July day in central Florida. Heat shimmers off the blacktop like waves over a stove. Walk fifty yards under a canopy of live oaks, though, and the air cools fast. City planners call that heat spike over paved streets the urban heat island effect. Growing proof shows that planting native trees is a smart buy for Florida towns.

First, wide tree crowns cool streets and cut summer power use. Leaves transpire water and block hot sun from brick walls and roads. As a result, shaded spots stay twenty to forty degrees cooler than bare lots. Studies in coastal municipalities found that homes shaded by mature live oaks used markedly less cooling power in August heat waves. Those savings shrink bills and ease strain on power lines.

Critics sometimes argue that street trees cost too much to trim and drop limbs in storms. Those concerns call for smart planning, not giving up on city trees. Wind-resistant Florida natives like live oak, bald cypress, and sable palm hold firm when given wide soil beds. Shallow-rooted ornamentals tucked into tiny sidewalk cuts fail far more often in high winds.

Tree canopies also clean storm rain before it flows into ponds and springs. Deep roots break up compacted city dirt so rain soaks down into the ground. Without roots, runoff washes motor oil and trash straight into creeks. When town leaders fund native trees and routine trims, they are not just buying nice views. They are building living infrastructure that cools streets, guards clean water, and boosts town resilience.

sections.sourceNote: Original Literary Story · Grade 3 Narrative Practice
paragraphs: Each day after school, Mateo ran to the town garden behind his school. He checked his neat row of cherry tomatoes. All April, hot sun baked the sandy dirt. Soon the leaves drooped low like tired hats. On Tuesday, Ms. Alvarez hung a sign on the gate: "Dry Spell — Please Conserve!"

Mateo sighed and stared at the empty watering cans. Across the path, his friend Priya set a blue barrel under the shed’s metal spout. "You want to catch rain when the sky holds zero clouds?" Mateo asked, arms crossed. Priya wiped her brow and grinned. "When storm clouds roll off the bay, this tub will hold fifty pails. If not, that rain runs straight down the road drain."

Mateo doubted one barrel could help ten beds, yet he hated seeing his plants wilt. Next day he brought window screen from his granddad’s shed. It would keep stray leaves and bugs out of Priya’s tub. By Friday, two fourth graders joined in. Together they set a brass spigot near the base and stacked flat bricks below so cans fit underneath.

Saturday came with a sudden boom of thunder. Silver sheets of rain beat on the tin roof. Mateo and Priya stood by the oak tree watching clean water surge down the spout and fill the barrel to the brim. On Monday, Mateo turned the brass spigot and filled his can without using the city hose. Looking at the perky green tomato vines, he realized big problems shrink when neighbors prepare together.

sections.label: Passage 1 (Primary Source)
sections.title: Excerpt from Keeper Maria Mestre de los Dolores’s Notebook, 1859
sections.authorByline: Adapted Original Historical Diary Entry (Simulated Primary Account)
sections.sourceNote: Original Fictionalized Firsthand Account · Grade 4 Paired Set
paragraphs: October 14, 1859 — Before sunset, a northeast wind began rattling the brass latches inside the St. Augustine tower. My father always said a keeper must trust her ears as much as her eyes. By dusk, salt spray tapped against the curved glass panes like impatient fingers. That sound reminded me that coastal ships depend on our steady beam.

Each evening I climb the winding iron steps with a heavy copper can of lard oil. Trimming the woven cotton wicks takes calm hands. If a wick burns unevenly, black soot clouds the precious glass prisms. Tonight the storm gusted fiercely. Still, as I lit the central lamp, amber light spilled across the dark Atlantic breakers like a golden ribbon guiding sailors safely home.

sections.label: Passage 2 (Secondary Source)
sections.title: Guarding the First Coast: The Science of Early Lighthouses
sections.sourceNote: Original Informational Article · Secondary Historical Account
paragraphs: During the nineteenth century, Florida’s Atlantic shoreline posed serious hazards for wooden ships. Shifting sandbars and shallow reefs waited just beneath the waves near St. Augustine. To warn captains away from danger, lighthouses used a remarkable optical invention called the Fresnel lens. This beehive-shaped frame of concentric glass prisms focused a single flame into a beam visible for miles.

Maintaining that beacon demanded exhausting daily labor. Keepers hauled gallons of fuel oil up narrow spiral staircases and polished hundreds of glass edges. Every few hours, they wound heavy clockwork weights so the revolving lens never stalled. Automated electric lamps replaced oil burners in the twentieth century. Still, historical records show that early keepers’ careful routines saved countless ships along Florida’s coast.

paragraphs: South Florida holds a wide, shallow sheet of moving water called the Everglades. Visitors gaze at miles of tall, gold-green blades swaying in the warm breeze. Many assume they see ordinary marsh grass. Most of that vast sea is sawgrass. This tough, sharp-edged sedge has shaped the Everglades ecosystem for thousands of years.

Look close at the edge of one sawgrass blade. You will soon spot how the plant got its name. Tiny, sawlike teeth line both sides of each leaf. Those stiff ridges shield the plant from hungry marsh grazers. They also catch morning dew and guide rain down to the roots. Under the dark, muddy peat, thick stems store energy even when the dry season leaves the ground cracked and parched.

For years, many folks thought every marsh fire was a bad event. They feared fire ruined wild homes for good. Scientists later learned the truth. Sawgrass hides live buds safe under wet mud. Mild winter fires burn off dead thatch without hurting those roots. Soon after the smoke clears, new green shoots push up through the ash. Bright sun reaches the water again for wading birds and small fish.

Today, park rangers plan prescribed burns in cool winter months. Winds stay mild and predictable then. Crews check damp soil and weather maps before each burn. Their careful steps help sawgrass marshes stay fresh and thick. What once looked like ruin turns out to be a dependable tool for keeping Florida’s River of Grass healthy.

sections.sourceNote: Original Informational Argument · Grade 5 Science & Civics
paragraphs: Step onto a wide asphalt lot on a July day in central Florida. Heat shimmers off the blacktop like waves over a stove. Walk fifty yards under a canopy of live oaks, though, and the air cools fast. City planners call that heat spike over paved streets the urban heat island effect. Growing proof shows that planting native trees is a smart buy for Florida towns.

First, wide tree crowns cool streets and cut summer power use. Leaves transpire water and block hot sun from brick walls and roads. As a result, shaded spots stay twenty to forty degrees cooler than bare lots. Studies in coastal municipalities found that homes shaded by mature live oaks used markedly less cooling power in August heat waves. Those savings shrink bills and ease strain on power lines.

Critics sometimes argue that street trees cost too much to trim and drop limbs in storms. Those concerns call for smart planning, not giving up on city trees. Wind-resistant Florida natives like live oak, bald cypress, and sable palm hold firm when given wide soil beds. Shallow-rooted ornamentals tucked into tiny sidewalk cuts fail far more often in high winds.

Tree canopies also clean storm rain before it flows into ponds and springs. Deep roots break up compacted city dirt so rain soaks down into the ground. Without roots, runoff washes motor oil and trash straight into creeks. When town leaders fund native trees and routine trims, they are not just buying nice views. They are building living infrastructure that cools streets, guards clean water, and boosts town resilience.

paragraphs: Each day after school, Mateo ran to the town garden behind his school. He checked his neat row of cherry tomatoes. All April, hot sun baked the sandy dirt. Soon the leaves drooped low like tired hats. On Tuesday, Ms. Alvarez hung a sign on the gate: "Dry Spell — Please Conserve!"

Mateo sighed and stared at the empty watering cans. Across the path, his friend Priya set a blue barrel under the shed’s metal spout. "You want to catch rain when the sky holds zero clouds?" Mateo asked, arms crossed. Priya wiped her brow and grinned. "When storm clouds roll off the bay, this tub will hold fifty pails. If not, that rain runs straight down the road drain."

Mateo doubted one barrel could help ten beds, yet he hated seeing his plants wilt. Next day he brought window screen from his granddad’s shed. It would keep stray leaves and bugs out of Priya’s tub. By Friday, two fourth graders joined in. Together they set a brass spigot near the base and stacked flat bricks below so cans fit underneath.

Saturday came with a sudden boom of thunder. Silver sheets of rain beat on the tin roof. Mateo and Priya stood by the oak tree watching clean water surge down the spout and fill the barrel to the brim. On Monday, Mateo turned the brass spigot and filled his can without using the city hose. Looking at the perky green tomato vines, he realized big problems shrink when neighbors prepare together.
